messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was twenty-five when he first came to the clinic on a Tuesday afternoon, his supervisor at the downtown hotel having finally insisted he speak to someone after he'd called out sick for the third time in two weeks. He sat in the waiting room in his housekeeping uniform—navy polo, name tag slightly crooked—and his leg bounced steadily against the linoleum floor. When he spoke, his voice was steady but his hands moved constantly, fingers picking at the hem of his shirt.

The trauma had begun when Marcus was seven. His father's boyfriend, Derek, moved into their apartment in late autumn. By winter, what had seemed like occasional roughness—a hard grip on the arm, a shove into the hallway—had become systematic. One night in January, Marcus had wet the bed. Derek's response was to drag him from under the covers, strip the sheets, and force Marcus's face down against the bare plastic mattress—the kind with a peculiar synthetic smell and a slick, grainy texture that Marcus could still feel against his cheek and forehead when he closed his eyes. The man held him there in the dark, pressing down, while Marcus couldn't breathe properly and didn't know if it would end. It did, eventually, but the pattern continued in different forms until Marcus was eleven and his mother finally left with him. By then, something fundamental had shifted in how Marcus understood the world.

Now, eighteen years later, Marcus lived alone in a studio apartment but never stayed there after dark. He would arrive home from his shift at the hotel around three in the afternoon, complete whatever tasks he needed to complete, and then leave again—to the twenty-four-hour diner, to a friend's place, to anywhere that had light and other people. When he did sleep, it was usually on his couch with the television on, the volume low but constant, because silence and darkness still felt like a trap closing around him. He had come to believe that he was marked—that something about what had happened to him was visible on his skin, that people looking at him could somehow see the shape of his humiliation. He felt, most of the time, like a thing rather than a person, as though the substance of who he was had been replaced by something hollow and used.

The nightmares had started a few years ago, intensifying in the past six months. They came almost every night—the memory of that mattress, the pressure, the dark, the feeling of being held down. But they weren't just dreams; they were vivid replays that felt completely real, with the texture against his skin, the smell, the inability to move. Sometimes he would wake up gasping, convinced for several seconds that he was still there, still being held. Other times the memory would surface during the day—triggered by a child crying in one of the hotel hallways, or by the particular weave of a rough blanket he encountered while changing beds—and the emotion would hit him so suddenly and with such force that he would have to step into a supply closet and wait for it to pass, his whole body shaking.

What had finally driven Marcus to call the clinic was a shift change at work. He'd been assigned to the night housekeeping rotation, which meant arriving at the hotel at ten p.m. The first two nights, he'd experienced what felt like constant panic—hyperaware of every shadow, every sound, his body flooding with adrenaline at the slightest movement. On the third night, a guest's child had cried from behind a closed door as Marcus was cleaning the hallway. He'd abandoned his cart, clocked out, and left the building. He hadn't returned. His supervisor had called him the next morning, and Marcus had found himself unable to explain. How could he say that the dark was dangerous, that he couldn't trust anyone, that being alone with another person—even a supervisor trying to help—made his chest tight with a fear he couldn't name?

He sat across from the therapist now, still in his work uniform, and admitted quietly that he didn't know how to live like this anymore. He was afraid of the night. He was afraid of being seen. He was afraid of what would happen if he stopped running.
